Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector-valued functions, $u(t)$ is a scalar function, and $\alpha$ and $\mathbf c$ are scalar and vector constants, respectively.

When working with vector functions, there are two types of products: the dot product and the cross product. So, there are two **product rules** for derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f\cdot g)^{'}(t)=f(t)\cdot {g}^{'}(t)+{f}^{'}(t)\cdot g(t)\, & \text{dot product rule} \\ (f\times g)^{'}(t)={f}^{'}(t)\times g(t)+f(t)\times {g}^{'}(t)\, & \text{cross product rule}\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** Remember that the cross product is anticommutative, meaning that $\mathbf f \times \mathbf g = - \mathbf g \times \mathbf f.$ Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\mathbf f \times \mathbf g)(t) = -\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\mathbf g \times \mathbf f)(t).
$$

When applying the cross product rule, the order in which the operations are applied is important.

If a surface is parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

where $(u,v) \in D\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ then the **fundamental vector product** of the surface is defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v = 
\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂u} \\ \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

In particular, if the fundamental vector product of a surface is nonzero at a point $(x_0, y_0),$ then it defines a normal vector to the surface at this point.

Let's find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle \sqrt{2}\cos{u}, \: \sqrt{2}\sin{u}, \: v \big\rangle.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u^2, \:u-v, \: v \big\rangle,
$$

Let $S$ be a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane. We wish to show that the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,\textrm d S = \iint\limits_D  \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

Let's consider a partition $P_1 \times P_2$ of the domain $D,$ where 

$$
P_1 = \left\{u_0,u_1,\ldots, u_m\right\},\qquad P_2 = \left\{v_0,v_1,\ldots, v_n\right\},
$$

and

$$
\Delta u_i = u_{i} - u_{i-1}, \qquad \Delta v_j = v_{j} - v_{j-1}.
$$

This partition generates a curved grid on the surface, as shown below.

![](images/8d/8d31bced1b87e460ec115f97b69a51d21261184b52011e26f32a00487e7cd2d1.png)

Now consider a "patch" $S_{ij}$ of the surface that corresponds to the rectangle $R_{ij}$ of the partition. How can we approximate the area of this small patch?

First, let's make a bigger picture of $S_{ij}.$

![](images/a1/a125124ac911c9e0557760d9f29ed7ae829f6595be58fec4f2ba39989e51f51b.png)

Here, we assume that the grid curves ${\color{blue}C_u}$ with equation $\mathbf{r}(u,v_j)$ and ${\color{red}C_v}$ with equation $\mathbf{r}(u_i,v)$ pass through the point $P_{ij}$ with position vector $\mathbf{r}(u_i,v_j).$

We now proceed to find a parallelogram whose area is approximately equal to the area of our patch.

- The vector that connects the bottom-left and bottom-right vertices of our patch is given by

$$
\mathbf r(u_{i+1}, v_j) - \mathbf r (u_i, v_j).
$$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated using a partial derivative, this vector is approximately equal to

$$
\mathbf{r}'_u(u_i,v_j) \Delta{u}_i,
$$

which is the vector that spans the bottom edge of the parallelogram shown in the diagram.

- Similarly, the vector that connects the bottom-left and top-left vertices of our patch is given by

$$
\mathbf r(u_{i}, v_{j+1}) - \mathbf r (u_i, v_j).
$$

This vector is approximately equal to

$$
\mathbf{r}'_v(u_i,v_j) \Delta{v}_j,
$$

which is the vector that spans the left edge of the parallelogram shown in the diagram.

As a result, we can approximate the area of $S_{ij}$ by the area of the parallelogram spanned by these two vectors. The area of such a parallelogram equals the magnitude of the corresponding cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}A({S}_{ij}) & \approx ‖{r}_{u}^{'}({u}_{i},{v}_{j})Δ{u}_{i}\times {r}_{v}^{'}({u}_{i},{v}_{j})Δ{v}_{j}‖ \\  & =‖{r}_{u}^{'}({u}_{i},{v}_{j})\times {r}_{v}^{'}({u}_{i},{v}_{j})‖\,Δ{u}_{i}Δ{v}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Adding up the approximations for all patches, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A(S) & \approx {\sum }_{i=0}^{m}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n}A({S}_{ij}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=0}^{m}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n}‖{r}_{u}^{'}({u}_{i},{v}_{j})\times {r}_{v}^{'}({u}_{i},{v}_{j})‖\,Δ{u}_{i}Δ{v}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a Riemann sum, and the closer the points $P_{ij}$ are to each other, the better our approximation will be. So, in the limit as $m,n\to\infty$ (or $\Delta u_i, \Delta v_j \to 0),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'}‖\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'}‖\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=4 \\ x-2 &=y\,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+(x-2) & =4 \\ 2x-2 & =4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3.$ But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-2 \\ y & =3-2 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as $\left(3, 1\right).$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))]
$$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} 	= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) &=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned}

$$

$$

But why is this formula true? To understand why, remember that the volume of a parallelepiped can be obtained by multiplying the area of the base by the height.

To compute the volume, we will multiply the area of the base by the height. First, though, let's write down the expression for the height:

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =|{\text{proj}}_{b\times c}\,a| \\  & =|\frac{a\cdot (b\times c)}{|b\times c|}| \\  & =\frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

In this lesson, we will explore strategies for parametrizing cylinders. 

Parametrizing a cylinder is no more difficult than parametrizing its base curve. The only difference is that we need a *second* parameter to control the variation parallel to the cylinder's axis. This second parameter is usually allowed to vary arbitrarily. 

For example, consider the parabolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as

$$
y = 8x^2.
$$

Notice that $y = y(x)$ is an explicit function of $x.$ Therefore, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on this surface, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨x,\,8{x}^{2},\,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

And that's it! We have successfully found a parametrization of this cylinder. 

Note that, under this parametrization

- the parameter $x \in (-\infty,\infty)$ controls the movement along the base curve, and

- the parameter $z \in (-\infty,\infty)$ controls the movement parallel to the $z$-axis.

Let's see some more examples.

We wish to calculate the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

To do this, we use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm dt.
$$

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=\cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},$ along the curve $C$ we have that 

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad y = \sin{t}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))=y\,i+x\,j=\operatorname{sin}t\,i+\operatorname{cos}t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}t\,i+\operatorname{cos}t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)$ by taking the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{'}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}t\,i+\operatorname{cos}t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t\,i+\operatorname{cos}t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}t+{cos}^{2}t \\  & ={cos}^{2}t-{sin}^{2}t \\  & =\operatorname{cos}2t\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

When $C$ is a closed curve, there is always a well-defined notion of "inside" and "outside" $C.$ It is usually easy to determine which region is inside or outside an arbitrary closed curve using our natural intuition.

One important quantity that we often need when dealing with closed, oriented curves is the **outward-pointing unit normal vector,** usually denoted $\mathbf n$.

As the name suggests:

- $\mathbf n$ is normal (i.e., perpendicular) to the curve $C$ at *every* point,

- it is a unit vector (i.e., its magnitude equals $1$), and

- it always points in the outward direction.

Since $\mathbf n$ must be normal to $C$ at *every* point, it must vary as we move around $C.$ Therefore, it is usually written either as a function of the parameter space (i.e., $\mathbf n(t)$) or as a function of the coordinates of the points on $C$ (i.e., $\mathbf n(x,y)$). 

As a concrete example, let's consider the closed, positively oriented ellipse $C,$ parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = 3\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 2\sin t\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi).
$$

![](images/fe/fea4c20453e9c80493f5c5431859fd7918d75cbaa494ad0b3deeccacfae24019.png)

For convenience, we first express $\mathbf r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
\mathbf r(t) 
= {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( t ) \\ y ( t )\end{array} \right]}
= {\left[ \begin{array}{c}3 \cos   t \\ 2 \sin   t\end{array} \right]}
$$

Let's calculate the vector $\mathbf n$ for this curve. To do this, we follow three steps.

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector $\mathbf r'(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

A typical tangent vector for our curve is shown below.

![](images/10/10ae867f682158bce2098234210206d4d7eb811be780505ca1984fb9e9516a27.png)

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation is

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ - 1 & 0\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Rotating the vector $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise, we get the vector $\tilde{\mathbf n}(t),$ given by

$$
\tilde{\mathbf n}(t)
=
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ - 1 & 0\end{array} \right]}
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 3 \sin   t \\ 2 \cos   t\end{array} \right]}
=
 {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \cos   t \\ 3 \sin   t\end{array} \right]}.
$$

The vector $\tilde{\mathbf n}(t)$ is shown below:

![](images/7c/7ca9a18d78783a923b63fcc41a8bc41ccab5c4a12bb00f5c305e35e2e1bc40e5.png)

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

The vector $\tilde{\mathbf n}(t)$ in an outward-pointing normal vector, but it is not a unit vector. Therefore, we need to normalize it.

Notice that  

$$
||\mathbf r'(t)|| = \sqrt{(3\sin t)^2 + (2\cos t)^2} = \sqrt{9\sin^2 t + 4\cos^2 t}.
$$

Furthermore, the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of $\mathbf r'(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore, we can calculate our outward-pointing unit vector $\mathbf n$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}(t)}{||{r}^{′}(t)||} \\  & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t}}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the vector

$$
\mathbf n = \dfrac{2\cos t\,\mathbf i + 3\sin t\,\mathbf j}{\sqrt{9\sin^2 t + 4\cos^2 t}}
$$

gives us an outward-pointing unit normal vector to every point on our ellipse.

Just as the derivative of a function represents the slope of the tangent line to the function, the partial derivative of a function has a geometric interpretation as well.

To illustrate, consider the surface $z = f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2$ and the plane $x=3.$ The intersection of the surface and the plane forms a downward parabolic curve, as shown below. A point $P(3,2,5)$ is plotted and a tangent line is drawn through that point.

![](images/86/8619c41cd0caf04ae9ee9bcae61e31739d8da583793a67c1c87e00186c3ac417.png)

   

To find the slope of the tangent, we can compute the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(18-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =-2y \\ {\frac{∂f}{∂y}|}_{P} & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To verify that this result is correct, we can find the equation of the downward parabolic curve and then use single-variable calculus to compute the slope of the tangent line.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,y) & =18-{3}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\  & =9-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the downward parabolic curve is $z=g(y) = 9-y^2.$ In the $yz$-plane, this curve has the following graph:

![](images/e9/e982ef5d6d8d4fec9c64957d46f22cea2a85bd002595642f58700cf48cce4256.png)

To find the slope of the tangent to $g(y)$ at $P,$ we can use single-variable calculus. We differentiate $g(y)$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(y) & =-2y \\ {g}^{′}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to derive the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s =\int_{a}^{b} f(\mathbf r(t)) \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

To do this, we proceed in four steps, as follows:

**Step 1**: We break the integration path $C$ into a series of line segments.

We choose a finite number of points $P_0,$ $P_1,$ $\ldots,$ $P_n$ along $C$ and form the polygonal path

$$
\overline{P_0P_1} \cup \overline{P_1P_2} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{P_{n-1}P_n}.
$$

Our polygonal path is shown in the diagram below.

![](images/2d/2d320e6a0f63a823e049203203cbc13c210e80bc98aab5a53bcb4e5299240920.png)

**Step 2**: For each line segment, we approximate the area enclosed by $f(x,y)$ and $C$ between the two endpoints of the segment. To do this, we calculate the area of a rectangle formed by the segment and the surface $z=f(x,y).$

The width of each line segment is given by

$$
||\overline{P_{k-1}P_k}|| .
$$

If $P_k$ is at the tip of $\mathbf r(t_k),$ then by the mean value theorem,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖\overset{―}{{P}_{k-1}{P}_{k}}‖ & =‖{r}^{'}({c}_{k})‖({t}_{k}-{t}_{k-1}) \\  & =‖{r}^{'}({c}_{k})‖Δ{t}_{k}\end{aligned}
$$

for some intermediate point $c_k \in [t_{k-1}, t_k],$ where $\Delta t_k = t_k - t_{k-1}.$

Therefore, the area formed by the rectangle with a width of $\big\| \overline{P_{k-1}P_k} \big\|$ and a height of $f(c_k)$ is given by

$$
f(c_k) \| \mathbf r'(c_k)\|\Delta t_k.
$$

**Step 3**: We sum the areas of all of our small rectangles, which gives us an *approximation* of our line integral. We get

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s \approx \sum_{k=1}^{n} f(\mathbf r(c_k)) \| \mathbf{r}'(c_k) \| \Delta t_k.
$$

**Step 4**: We take the limit as the width of each rectangle tends to zero (or equivalently, as the number of rectangles tends to infinity). This gives us the exact representation of our line integral:

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s =\lim_{n\to\infty }\sum_{k=1}^{n} f(\mathbf r(c_k)) \| \mathbf{r}'(c_k) \| \Delta t_k = \int_{a}^{b} f(\mathbf r(t)) \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t
$$

Let's consider a surface $z=f(x,y)$ and a unit vector $\mathbf{u} = \left\langle  u_1, u_2 \right\rangle.$

The **directional derivative of $f$** at the point $(x_0,y_0)$ in the direction of $\mathbf{u}$ is

$$
f'_{\mathbf u}(x_0,y_0) = \lim\limits_{t \to 0}\dfrac{f(\mathbf x_0 + t \mathbf u) - f(\mathbf x_0)}{t}.
$$

The directional derivative of $f$ is the rate of change of the function $f$ in the direction of $\mathbf{u}.$ We'll discuss this idea more later in the lesson.

It turns out that if $f$ is differentiable, we can write $f'_{\mathbf u}$ in terms of partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y,$ as follows:

$$
f'_{\mathbf u}(x_0,y_0) = \nabla f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \mathbf u.
$$

At the end of the lesson, we'll derive this formula. But for now, let's get some practice using it.

For example, let's find the directional derivative of the function $f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2$ at the point $(x_0,y_0)=(1,2)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}.$

First, we find the unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ in the direction of $\mathbf{v} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $\nabla f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,2)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,2) & =(2\cdot 1)\,i+(2\cdot 2)\,j \\  & =2i+4j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,2) & =∇\,f(1,2)\cdot u \\  & =(2\,i+4\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}j) \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressed in component form, our vector is $\mathbf{a}=-2\mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j}.$

To find the magnitude (length) of $\mathbf{a},$ we can use the Pythagorean theorem on $\triangle OXA.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{XA}| & =|\,4\,|=4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\,| & =\sqrt{|\overset{\to }{OX}{|}^{2}+|\overset{\to }{XA}{|}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2u & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & v \\ 2v & u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2u & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-2{u}^{2},\,4uv⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-2{u}^{2},\,4uv⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-2{v}^{2})^{2}+(-2{u}^{2})^{2}+(4uv)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}+16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({u}^{4}+{v}^{4}+4{u}^{2}{v}^{2})} \\  & =2\sqrt{{u}^{4}+{v}^{4}+4{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\sqrt{{u}^{4}+{v}^{4}+4{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$

$$
